n: Isaiah begins like a singer at a harvest festival, offering a love song about his friend’s vineyard. The “wellbeloved” is the Lord, and the vineyard is Israel.

f.g: Dear friend; here the Lord Himself.

n: The owner did everything right: he dug and cleared the land, planted the best vines, built a watchtower and a winepress. But it produced only sour, wild grapes.

f.g: A watchtower to guard against thieves and animals.

n: Isaiah asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between the owner and his vineyard — not realizing they are judging themselves.
What more could the owner have done? Why did it produce bad fruit? Compare the Lord of the vineyard’s same question in Zenos’s allegory.

f.w: What could have been done more to my vineyard

n: So he will remove the hedge and wall, letting animals eat and trample it. Without God’s protection, Israel will be overrun.
He will let it go wild: no pruning or hoeing, only briers and thorns. He will even command the clouds not to rain on it — showing the owner is God.
The meaning is revealed: the vineyard is Israel and Judah. God looked for justice but found bloodshed, for righteousness but heard cries of the oppressed. In Hebrew these are striking wordplays.
The first of six woes: against wealthy landowners who buy up house after house and field after field, pushing out the poor until they live alone in the land.
The Lord swore to Isaiah that these great mansions will stand empty. 2 Nephi 15:9 reads “great and fair cities without inhabitant.”
The land will barely produce: ten acres of vineyard will yield only about six gallons of wine, and planted seed will produce a tenth of what was sown.

f.g: A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).
A dry measure, about 10 ephahs — so the harvest is one-tenth of the seed.
Literally “ten yoke” — what ten teams of oxen could plow in a day.

n: The second woe: against those who start drinking early in the morning and continue late into the night until they are inflamed with wine.

f.w: Woe unto them that rise up early

n: Their parties have music and wine, but they pay no attention to what the Lord is doing. Pleasure has made them spiritually blind.

f.g: A stringed instrument like a lyre.

n: Because they lack knowledge of God, the people will go into captivity. Both nobles and common people will suffer hunger and thirst.
The grave opens its mouth wide to swallow Jerusalem’s proud and partying crowds. Death is pictured as a hungry monster.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

n: Both common people and the powerful will be humbled, and the proud brought low.
Through righteous judgment, the Lord will show Himself exalted and holy.
Lambs will graze in the ruins of the rich, and strangers will eat in the deserted estates. The land grabbed by the greedy returns to pasture.
The third woe: against those who drag their sins along behind them like a cart pulled with ropes. They are bound to their sins and keep hauling them.
They mock God’s warnings, daring Him to hurry up and carry out His plan so they can see it. Scoffers often demand proof.
The fourth woe: against those who flip moral values, calling evil good and good evil. This warning feels especially relevant today.

f.w: call evil good, and good evil

n: The fifth woe: against those who think they are wiser than God.
The sixth woe: against those whose only “heroic” talent is drinking and mixing liquor. Isaiah mocks their false strength.
These same people take bribes to declare the guilty innocent and deny justice to the innocent.
Like fire burning straw, their roots will rot and their blossoms blow away as dust, because they have rejected the Lord’s law and despised His word.

f.g: Dry stalks left in a field after harvest.

n: The Lord’s anger has struck His people, yet His hand is still stretched out. In context this means continued judgment; Latter-day Saints also find hope in the phrase, since His hand remains extended to those who repent.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: The Lord will raise a banner for distant nations and whistle for them. Historically this summoned Assyria against Israel; Latter-day Saints also see the ensign as the restored gospel gathering Israel from afar.

f.g: A flag or signal pole raised on a hill to rally people.
Whistle, as a beekeeper or shepherd calls.

n: Those who come will be tireless, never stumbling, sleeping, or loosening their belts or sandal straps — always ready. Some Latter-day Saints see in this the energy of the latter-day gathering.

f.g: Belt; tightening it meant being ready to move.

n: Their arrows are sharp and bows ready; their horses’ hooves are hard as flint and their chariot wheels spin like a whirlwind.
They roar like lions seizing prey and carrying it off with no one able to rescue it — a picture of Assyria’s unstoppable armies.
In that day they will roar like the sea, and the land will be covered in darkness and distress, even the sky darkened.
